summary: A country in Central America, one of the core areas of the ancient Maya civilization, with the highest proportion of indigenous people in Central America, and home to famous sites such as Tikal.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1524 Pedro de Alvarado led a Spanish army that conquered the Maya kingdoms of Guatemala, and the Franciscans and Dominicans then began missionary work; from 1537 the Dominican Bartolomé de las Casas preached peacefully in the north, which is why that region became known as the "Land of True Peace" (Verapaz). Catholicism fused with Maya beliefs, producing folk cults such as that of San Simón (Maximón). After 1871 the Liberal government confiscated church property and expelled religious orders, weakening the church's power; during the civil war many clergy spoke up for the indigenous people, and in 1998 Bishop Gerardi was murdered two days after releasing a human rights report.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical)
ranking.description: In 1882 the Liberal president Justo Rufino Barrios invited American Presbyterians to preach in Guatemala in order to weaken the power of the Catholic Church. After the great earthquake of 1976, large numbers of American Evangelical groups came to provide relief and set up churches; the dictator Efraín Ríos Montt, who ruled in 1982–1983, was himself an Evangelical pastor. In the civil war and social turmoil, Evangelical churches provided networks of mutual aid and a sense of security, making Guatemala one of the countries with the highest proportion of Evangelicals in Latin America, and the capital has many large neo-Pentecostal churches.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious are found mainly in metropolitan areas such as Guatemala City, related to the rising education level of the younger generation and dissatisfaction with the church's role in politics and scandals, and their proportion has gradually increased in recent years.

ranking.name: Maya traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Maya traditional belief has calendar priests (aj q'ij) conduct ceremonies according to the 260-day sacred calendar, burning incense and praying on mountaintops, in caves and at altars. It was suppressed during colonization and the civil war, and gradually revived openly after the 1996 peace accords recognized the indigenous right to spiritual belief. Very few people identify as following only the Maya religion, but many Catholics and indigenous people take part in traditional ceremonies at the same time.

religion.background: Guatemala is a core region of the ancient Maya civilization, whose people worshipped gods such as the maize god and the rain god and used a sacred calendar. After the Spanish conquest of 1524, Catholicism became the state religion, but Maya belief continued in syncretic form. In the 19th century the Liberal reforms struck at the church and introduced Protestantism to counter Catholicism. In the civil war of 1960–1996 the indigenous people suffered large-scale violence, and religious groups acted either as shelters or as political participants. Evangelicals grew greatly around the time of the civil war, transforming Guatemala from a Catholic country into a society where Catholics and Protestants are evenly matched.

language.official: The official language is Spanish, and 22 Maya languages as well as Garifuna and Xinca are also recognized.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: After the Spanish conquest of 1524, Spanish became the language of colonial administration, the church and commerce, and the mixed-race Ladinos have it as their mother tongue. After independence in the 19th century the government promoted national education centered on Spanish as a tool of national integration. Today Spanish is the only nationwide official language, spoken mainly in the capital, the east and the Pacific coast.

ranking.name: Mayan languages (K'iche', Q'eqchi', Kaqchikel, Mam, etc.)
ranking.description: There are more than twenty Mayan languages in Guatemala, of which K'iche', Q'eqchi', Kaqchikel and Mam have the most speakers, mainly in the western and northern highlands. The Popol Vuh, written in K'iche' in the mid-16th century, is a classic of Maya literature. In the civil war of the 1980s the military's massacres of Maya communities such as the Ixil caused heavy casualties; after the 1996 peace accords the government passed the National Languages Law in 2003 recognizing the Mayan languages, but the shift of young people to Spanish is still widespread.

language.history: The Mayan languages of Guatemala can be traced back thousands of years, and the Classic Maya used hieroglyphic writing, leaving many inscriptions in cities such as Tikal. After the Spanish conquest, missionaries wrote Mayan languages in the Latin alphabet, and indigenous intellectuals also recorded classics such as the Popol Vuh. Under colonial rule and after independence the state long promoted Spanish, and Mayan languages were marginalized. The Academy of Mayan Languages established in 1990 and the 1996 peace accords promoted bilingual education and language rights, and the Nobel Peace Prize awarded in 1992 to the K'iche' Rigoberta Menchú also drew international attention to Maya culture.

ranking.name: Pepián
ranking.description: Chicken or beef stewed in a thick sauce blended from roasted pumpkin seeds, sesame, dried chilies, tomato and spices, served with rice and tortillas.
ranking.history: Pepián is regarded as one of Guatemala's national dishes, combining the ancient Maya technique of making sauces from roasted seeds and chilies with the chicken, beef and spices brought by the Spanish. It is a typical example of the fusion of Maya and Spanish food in the colonial period, is common at festivals and family gatherings, and has been listed as part of Guatemala's national cultural heritage.

ranking.name: Kak'ik (turkey soup)
ranking.description: A red spicy soup boiled from turkey meat with roasted tomato, dried chilies, cilantro and annatto seeds, served with corn tamales and rice.
ranking.history: Kak'ik is a traditional soup of the Q'eqchi' Maya of Alta Verapaz in the north, and the name comes from the Q'eqchi' language. The turkey is a fowl native to the Americas that was domesticated by the indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica, and in Maya culture it was often used in sacrifices and feasts. This soup is made on important occasions such as weddings and religious festivals and has been listed as part of Guatemala's national intangible cultural heritage, a representative of Maya food that continues to this day.

ranking.name: Fiambre (cold-cut salad)
ranking.description: A large platter of cold salad mixed from dozens of kinds of cold meats, sausages, cheeses, pickled vegetables, eggs and seafood, colorful and astonishingly large.
ranking.history: Fiambre is made only around All Saints' Day on November 1 and All Souls' Day on the 2nd each year. Traditionally, on these two days families go to the cemetery to tend graves and bring flowers for the dead, taking fiambre to share with family; folklore says it originated from the dishes each family brought to the cemetery being mixed together. It combines the meats and curing techniques brought by Spanish colonization with the festival traditions of Catholicism, and each family has its own secret recipe.

ranking.name: Tamales
ranking.description: Corn dough filled with pork or chicken stewed in tomato sauce, wrapped in plantain or corn leaves and steamed, with a moist, creamy texture and the fresh fragrance of the leaves.
ranking.history: Tamales are one of the oldest foods of Central America; Maya murals of about two thousand years ago at the San Bartolo site in Guatemala depict similar food, and maize was a sacred crop in Maya culture, with the Popol Vuh even recording that humans were created from maize. After colonization new ingredients such as pork and chicken were added. Today Guatemalans always eat tamales on Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve, and eating tamales on Saturday morning is also a habit in many families.

ranking.name: Chile relleno
ranking.description: Bell peppers are deseeded, filled with a stuffing of minced meat stir-fried with vegetables such as carrot and green beans, coated in egg batter and fried, then topped with tomato sauce.
ranking.history: The origin of chile relleno is linked with the colonial-era cuisine of Puebla in Mexico, combining the native American chili with the pork, eggs and frying techniques introduced by the Spanish. The Guatemalan version mostly uses milder bell peppers, with plenty of vegetables in the filling. It is a common dish at family lunches and small restaurants, is often put in bread to make a street snack, and is also popular during Holy Week.
